# Working with Data in R {#sec-working-with-data}

```{r}
#| include: false
#| eval: true
# console() renders a code listing plus the console session it produces.
source("_console.R")
suppressMessages({library(dplyr); library(readr); library(tidyr)})
# Examples in this chapter run against this data frame. Students load it
# themselves with read_csv("data/field_yields.csv"); the path differs here
# because the book renders from the project root.
yields <- readr::read_csv("practice/data/field_yields.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

In the last chapter, we created small datasets directly in R. Real data analysis usually
starts somewhere else: with a file. That creates a few practical questions. Where should the
file go? How does R find it? How do we bring it into R? And once it is there, how do we
check that R has read it correctly?

This chapter develops a simple workflow for working with real data: keep everything for an
analysis in one project folder, refer to files with relative paths, use packages to add
functions to R, read the data from a CSV file, inspect it before doing any analysis, and
recognize whether it is organized in a useful shape. These habits are not exciting, but they
prevent a remarkable number of problems later.

## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

::: {.objectives}
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

1. Set up a self-contained project folder for an analysis.
2. Explain the difference between an absolute and a relative path.
3. Install and load an R package, and explain the difference between the two.
4. Read a CSV file into R as a data frame.
5. Inspect a new dataset and identify common problems.
6. Calculate basic summary statistics while handling missing values correctly.
7. Explain what tidy data means and recognize data that needs to be reshaped.
:::

## One Folder Per Project {#sec-project-folder}

Before we read any data into R, we need somewhere to put it. A good rule: keep everything
for one analysis inside one project folder. Suppose we are analyzing a canola variety trial.
Our folder might look like this:

```
canola-trial/
  data/
    canola_trial.csv          <- exactly as it arrived
  R/
    01_clean.R
    02_analysis.R
  output/
    yield_by_variety.png
    summary_table.csv
  README.md
```

`data/` contains the original data; `R/` contains the scripts, numbered in the order they
run; `output/` contains tables, figures, and other results the scripts produce; and
`README.md` holds notes explaining the project. The exact folder names matter less than the
principle: **the project is self-contained**. If you zip `canola-trial/` and send it to
somebody else, they have everything they need to run your analysis. A script that reaches
out to a file elsewhere on your hard drive will not travel like that.

**Raw data is never edited.**  Suppose `canola_trial.csv` contains an obvious typo. You
could open the file in Excel, fix the cell, and save -- but then there is no record of what
you changed, and you have written over the only copy of what you were given. Keep the
original file exactly as it arrived and make the correction in your R script, where it
leaves a trail: what changed, and how.

**Outputs are disposable.**  The opposite principle applies to `output/`: everything there
should be something your scripts can recreate. Deleting the contents of `output/` and seeing
whether your scripts regenerate everything is a useful test of whether an analysis is
reproducible.

To make this work, open the project folder itself in Positron at the start of a session:
**File → Open Folder…**, then choose the folder containing `data/`, `R/`, and `output/`. R
now treats this folder as its starting point when it looks for files, which makes the paths
in the next section much simpler.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why this matters for AI

AI coding assistants also work better when the relevant scripts and files are organized
together. When we use AI tools later in the book (Module 5), a well-organized project gives
the assistant useful context about the analysis.
:::


## Packages {#sec-packages}

R comes with hundreds of useful functions. Other people have written thousands more and
bundled them into **packages** -- add-ons that give R additional functions. Using a package
is a two-step process:

1. **Install it -- once per computer.** This downloads the package from the internet and saves it on your machine:

    ```r
    install.packages("tidyverse")
    ```

    The first installation can take a few minutes and prints a *lot* of messages. Some appear in red even when nothing has gone wrong; what matters is whether R ultimately reports an error.

2. **Load it -- once per script.** Installing puts the package on your computer, but it is not switched on until you *load* it. Put this at the top of every script that uses the tidyverse:

    ```r
    library(tidyverse)
    ```

If you skip the `library()` step and try to use a package function, R will stop with an error like:

```
Error in read_csv(...) : could not find function "read_csv"
```

That "could not find function" message almost always means you forgot to load the package (or you have not installed it yet). The fix is to run `library(tidyverse)` first. Note the quirk: you put quotes around the name when you *install* (`install.packages("tidyverse")`) but not when you *load* (`library(tidyverse)`). The reason is not important yet; just recognize the pattern.

## The Tidyverse {#sec-tidyverse}

The package we will use most is actually a collection of packages called the **tidyverse**.
Different tidyverse packages do different jobs, and four will matter most in this book:

| Package   | Main job          |
|-----------|-------------------|
| `readr`   | reading data      |
| `dplyr`   | manipulating data |
| `tidyr`   | reshaping data    |
| `ggplot2` | making graphs     |

Installing the tidyverse installs these and several others, and `library(tidyverse)` loads
the core packages at once. The tidyverse has become the standard way of working with tabular
data in R, and it is what this book uses: its packages share a consistent style and provide
particularly convenient tools for tables of data.

Base R can do many of the same things, and you will see base functions in documentation,
online examples, and AI-generated code. There is nothing wrong with mixing the two. In this
chapter we use `readr` to bring data into R; in the next chapter we use `dplyr` to
manipulate it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Other resources — packages and the tidyverse

- **R for Data Science (2nd ed.)** -- the [Introduction](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/intro.html) describes the tidyverse workflow (import → tidy → transform → visualize → model → communicate) this course follows.
- **tidyverse.org** -- [the package index](https://www.tidyverse.org/packages/) lists the core packages and what each does.
:::

## Reading Data from CSV {#sec-reading-data}

The dataset for this chapter and the next is
[`field_yields.csv`](practice/data/field_yields.csv) -- 60 canola fields with columns
`field_id`, `region`, `variety`, `acres`, `yield_bu_acre`, `year`, `seeding_date`, and
`units`. Download it and put it in your project's `data/` folder, and make sure you have
opened the project folder itself in Positron.

Start your script by loading the tidyverse, then read the file:

```r
library(tidyverse)

yields <- read_csv("data/field_yields.csv")
```

Read the second line from right to left: read `field_yields.csv` from the `data` folder, and
save the resulting data frame as `yields`. After running it, `yields` is an object in R.

`read_csv` also prints a short note about the **column types** it guessed -- numeric,
character, date, and so on. R guesses well but not perfectly, which is one reason we always
inspect a dataset after reading it.


## Paths, and Why `setwd()` Is a Trap {#sec-paths}

A **path** tells R where to find a file.  There are two kinds.

An **absolute path** gives the file's complete location on one computer:

```r
read_csv("/Users/peter/Documents/canola-trial/data/canola_trial.csv")
```

A **relative path** describes the location relative to the project folder:

```r
read_csv("data/canola_trial.csv")
```

The second version is much better. The absolute path contains information specific to one
computer: the username `peter`, the location of the Documents folder, and the operating
system's folder layout. If I send that script to you, you probably do not have
`/Users/peter/Documents/`. But if we both have the same project folder, we both have
`data/canola_trial.csv`. So the rule is: open the project folder in Positron, and use
relative paths inside your scripts.

R does have a function, `setwd()`, that changes the working directory from inside a script:

```r
setwd("/Users/peter/Documents/canola-trial")     # do not do this
```

You will see this in old scripts and online examples. Do not put a line like it in a script
you intend to share: it solves the path problem on your computer by creating a path problem
on everybody else's. This is the most common reason a script that works fine for its author
fails for everyone else.

If you are ever unsure where R thinks it is, run `getwd()` ("get working directory"). R
prints the folder it is currently treating as its starting point.

::: {.callout-note}
## Windows note

Windows displays paths with backslashes, as in `C:\Users\Peter\Documents`, but a backslash
means something special inside an R string. Write forward slashes even on Windows:
`"C:/Users/Peter/Documents"`. R handles the translation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## File names

Two rules save a lot of trouble. Use short descriptive names without spaces or punctuation:
`yield_data_final.csv`, not `Field Yields FINAL!!.csv`. And write dates as YYYY-MM-DD:
`2026-09-15_deliveries.csv` sorts chronologically on its own, and `Sept15.csv` does not.

If you find yourself writing `final`, `final_v2`, `final_REAL` in file names, the project
needs version control rather than longer file names. Git is the common system; we will not
cover it here.
:::

### When R cannot find the file {.unnumbered}

A common error looks like this:

```
Error: 'data/field_yields.csv' does not exist in current working directory (...)
```

Do not start changing the code randomly. Check two things, in order:

- **Did you open the correct project folder?** **File → Open Folder…** in Positron; the
  folder you open should contain `data/`.
- **Where does R think it is?** Run `getwd()` and look at the folder it prints. Starting
  from that folder, can you go into a folder called `data` and find `field_yields.csv`? If
  yes, the path works.

### A few related functions {.unnumbered}

CSV means comma-separated values, but text data can be separated in other ways. `read_csv2`
reads files that use semicolons; `read_tsv` reads tab-separated files. And `write_csv` is
the mirror image of `read_csv` -- one brings data into R, the other writes it out:

```r
write_csv(yields, "output/yields_clean.csv")
```

### Inspecting the data {.unnumbered}

Successfully reading a file does not mean you are ready to analyze it. Inspect it first:

```r
yields              # prints the data frame (first 10 rows)
head(yields)        # first 6 rows
nrow(yields)        # number of rows
ncol(yields)        # number of columns
names(yields)       # column names
glimpse(yields)     # compact column-by-column view, with types
summary(yields)     # quick summary of every column
```

`glimpse()` shows each column and its type; `summary()` reports the min, max, mean, median,
and quartiles of every numeric column. The goal is not to run these commands mechanically
but to answer some questions:

- Did I get the number of observations I expected?
- Are the variables I expected actually present?
- Did R interpret numeric variables as numbers?
- Are the values in plausible ranges?
- Are there missing values?

Looking at the data before analyzing it catches many mistakes cheaply.

### Viewing Data in Positron {#sec-data-explorer .unnumbered}

You can also inspect the data visually. After you run the `read_csv` line, `yields` appears
in the **Variables** pane. Click it and Positron opens the **Data Explorer**: a
spreadsheet-style view of the data.

<!-- TODO(Peter): screenshot of the Variables pane with `yields` listed after read_csv.
![After reading the file, `yields` appears in the Variables pane. Clicking it opens the Data Explorer.](images/positron_variables_yields.png){#fig-variables-yields}
-->

<!-- TODO(Peter): screenshot of the Data Explorer open on field_yields.
![The Data Explorer: the data in a spreadsheet-style grid, with a summary column profile down the left.](images/positron_data_explorer.png){#fig-data-explorer}
-->

The Data Explorer has two parts. The grid shows the rows and columns, and you can sort and
filter them by clicking the column headers. The summary panel shows, for each column, its
type, the percentage of missing values, and a small sketch of its distribution. Some
problems are much easier to notice by looking at the data than by reading console output.

There is one important difference from Excel: the Data Explorer is for viewing data, not
fixing it. You cannot change a cell. The file in `data/` stays as it arrived, and any
correction happens in the script, where it is recorded.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Summary Statistics in R {#sec-r-summary-stats}

Once the data are in R, we can calculate the same summary statistics we used in Excel.
`yield_bu_acre` is a column of the data frame `yields`, so we refer to it as
`yields$yield_bu_acre`:

```r
mean(yields$yield_bu_acre)
median(yields$yield_bu_acre)
sd(yields$yield_bu_acre)
var(yields$yield_bu_acre)
min(yields$yield_bu_acre)
max(yields$yield_bu_acre)
range(yields$yield_bu_acre)              # returns c(min, max)
quantile(yields$yield_bu_acre, 0.25)
quantile(yields$yield_bu_acre, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))  # multiple at once
IQR(yields$yield_bu_acre)
```

The statistical ideas have not changed since Module 1; only the way we ask the computer to
calculate them has.

### Missing values {.unnumbered}

Real datasets often contain missing observations, which R represents as `NA`. Some of our 60
fields are missing a yield, so this happens:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
console('
mean(yields$yield_bu_acre)

mean(yields$yield_bu_acre, na.rm = TRUE)
')
```

The first call says: calculate the mean of these observations. One of them is unknown, so R
cannot calculate the mean, and it returns `NA` rather than silently discarding information.
The second call, with `na.rm = TRUE` ("remove NAs"), says: calculate the mean using the
observations that are not missing. That may be exactly what we want -- but now the decision
is visible in the code.

This is an important difference from Excel, where many functions skip blank cells
automatically. Neither behavior solves the underlying statistical problem of missing data;
for now, the point is that if R unexpectedly returns `NA`, check whether your data contains
missing values. We return to missing data properly when we clean datasets in @sec-cleaning.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

- **Video** -- Dr E Research Videos, [*Basic summary statistics in R*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8XFmPP93w_Y) -- mean, median, standard deviation, and the number summary.
:::

## Tidy Data {#sec-tidy-data}

Before analyzing a dataset, we also need to think about its shape. The tidyverse is built
around an idea called **tidy data** [@r4ds]. A dataset is tidy when:

1. Every variable has its own **column**.
2. Every observation has its own **row**.
3. Every value has its own **cell**.

For example, this dataset is tidy:

```
  region  crop   yield
  South   Canola    41
  South   Wheat     52
  South   Barley    64
  Central Canola    44
  Central Wheat     55
  Central Barley    68
```

An observation here is a region-crop combination; the variables are `region`, `crop`, and
`yield`. Each variable has a column and each observation has a row.

Now compare this version of the same data:

```
  region  Canola Wheat Barley
  South       41    52     64
  Central     44    55     68
```

This table is easier for a person to read, but it is not tidy. Canola, Wheat, and Barley are
not three different variables; they are three values of the variable `crop`. This is the
wide-versus-long distinction from @sec-wide-long, where a PivotTable needed the long form.
For analysis in R, the long form is usually the more convenient one, because `crop` is an
ordinary variable that R can filter by, group by, and compare.

### Recognizing untidy data {.unnumbered}

Some common warning signs:

- **Values stored in column names.** A table with columns `region`, `2024`, `2025`, `2026`,
  where the year columns hold yields. The years are values of a variable called `year`; the
  tidy version has columns `region`, `year`, `yield`.
- **More than one variable in a column.** A `region_variety` column containing
  `"South_InVigor"`. That is two variables, `region` and `variety`, in one column.
- **One observation spread over several rows.** Price in one row and quantity in another row
  for the same market and year.

What counts as an observation depends on the dataset and the question, but the basic test is
always the same: what does one row represent? You should be able to answer that. When you
first open a dataset, ask what one row represents, what each column represents, whether any
values are hiding in column names, and whether any column holds several variables at once.

Reshaping a dataset between the wide and long forms is done by a pair of functions,
`pivot_longer` and `pivot_wider`, covered with the rest of the cleaning toolkit in
@sec-reshaping. For now, the goal is to recognize the shape that analysis wants.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Other resources — tidy data

- **R for Data Science (2nd ed.)** -- [Chapter 5, "Data tidying"](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-tidy) develops the tidy-data idea and shows how datasets are reshaped between long and wide forms.
- **Video** -- Riffomonas Project, [*Reshaping data to be long or wide with pivot_longer and pivot_wider*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZVddiwrbrr4).
:::

## Column Names {#sec-renaming}

Column names matter because we type them repeatedly. Real datasets sometimes arrive with
names like `Yield (bu/ac)`, `REGION_NAME`, or `Field ID Number` -- readable to a person, but
awkward in code. This book prefers names like `yield_bu_ac`, `region`, and `field_id`:
lowercase, words separated by underscores, short but descriptive. This style is called
**snake_case**.

You do not need to fix every imperfect name immediately. But when you inspect a new dataset
with `names()`, look for names that will make the analysis unnecessarily awkward. The next
chapter shows how to rename columns in code, and @sec-cleaning covers cleaning up a whole
set of bad names at once.

## Putting the Workflow Together {#sec-data-workflow}

The whole chapter fits in one short script. Suppose the project contains:

```
field-yields/
  data/
    field_yields.csv
  R/
    01_explore.R
  output/
```

Open `field-yields/` in Positron and create `R/01_explore.R`:

```r
# ---
# Title: Explore field yield data
# Author: Your Name
# Date: 2026-09-29
# ---

# Load packages
library(tidyverse)

# Read data
yields <- read_csv("data/field_yields.csv")

# Inspect structure
nrow(yields)
names(yields)
glimpse(yields)

# Inspect values
summary(yields)

# Summarize yield
mean(yields$yield_bu_acre, na.rm = TRUE)
median(yields$yield_bu_acre, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(yields$yield_bu_acre, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Notice what the script does not contain: no `setwd()`, no reliance on manually edited data,
and no jump straight from reading the file to analysis without checking what came in. It
follows the workflow this chapter has been building: open the project, load packages, read
the data, inspect it, check for problems, and only then analyze.

In the next chapter, we learn how to manipulate the data itself: selecting columns,
filtering rows, creating variables, sorting observations, and calculating summaries for
groups.
